title: How do you find the correct balance of vibecoding?
author: Topango_Dev
selftext: opus 5.5 and gpt 6 astra are very impressive, my skills are nowhere near what they can do and it makes spending 3 yrs for 5% of that knowledge feel pointless, its way more fun to just have claude/gpt make my custom systems but i dont want to be one of those people that doesnt understand what they've even made, should i just know the architecture and have AI do the code? or should i just know a little bit? or all of it?

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
Pay heed: 

>*You just went to the Google home page.*  
  
*Simple, isn’t it? What just actually happened?*  
  
*Well, when you know a bit of about how browsers work, it’s not quite that simple. You’ve just put into play HTTP, HTML, CSS, ECMAscript, and more. Those are actually such incredibly complex technologies that they’ll make any engineer dizzy if they think about them too much, and such that no single company can deal with that entire complexity.*  
  
*Let’s simplify.*  
  
*You just connected your computer to www.google.com.*  
  
*Simple, isn’t it? What just actually happened?*  
  
*Well, when you know a bit about how networks work, it’s not quite that simple. You’ve just put into play DNS, TCP, UDP, IP, Wifi, Ethernet, DOCSIS, OC, SONET, and more. Those are actually such incredibly complex technologies that they’ll make any engineer dizzy if they think about them too much, and such that no single company can deal with that entire complexity.*  
  
*Let’s simplify.*  
  
*You just typed* [*www.google.com*](http://www.google.com) *in the location bar of your browser.*  
  
*Simple, isn’t it? What just actually happened?*  
  
*Well, when you know a bit about how operating systems work, it’s not quite that simple. You’ve just put into play a kernel, a USB host stack, an input dispatcher, an event handler, a font hinter, a sub-pixel rasterizer, a windowing system, a graphics driver, and more, all of those written in high-level languages that get processed by compilers, linkers, optimizers, interpreters, and more. Those are actually such incredibly complex technologies that they’ll make any engineer dizzy if they think about them too much, and such that no single company can deal with that entire complexity.*  
  
*Let’s simplify.*  
  
*You just pressed a key on your keyboard.*  
  
*Simple, isn’t it? What just actually happened?*  
  
*Well, when you know a bit about how input peripherals work, it’s not quite that simple. You’ve just put into play a power regulator, a debouncer, an input multiplexer, a USB device stack, a USB hub stack, all of that implemented in a single chip. That chip is built around thinly sliced wafers of highly purified single-crystal silicon ingot, doped with minute quantities of other atoms that are blasted into the crystal structure, interconnected with multiple layers of aluminum or copper, that are deposited according to patterns of high-energy ultraviolet light that are focused to a precision of a fraction of a micron, connected to the outside world via thin gold wires, all inside a packaging made of a dimensionally and thermally stable resin. The doping patterns and the interconnects implement transistors, which are grouped together to create logic gates. In some parts of the chip, logic gates are combined to create arithmetic and bitwise functions, which are combined to create an ALU. In another part of the chip, logic gates are combined into bistable loops, which are lined up into rows, which are combined with selectors to create a register bank. In another part of the chip, logic gates are combined into bus controllers and instruction decoders and microcode to create an execution scheduler. In another part of the chip, they’re combined into address and data multiplexers and timing circuitry to create a memory controller. There’s even more. Those are actually such incredibly complex technologies that they’ll make any engineer dizzy if they think about them too much, and such that no single company can deal with that entire complexity.*  
  
*Can we simplify further?*  
  
*In fact, very scarily, no, we can’t. We can barely comprehend the complexity of a single chip in a computer keyboard, and yet there’s no simpler level. The next step takes us to the software that is used to design the chip’s logic, and that software itself has a level of complexity that requires to go back to the top of the loop.*  
  
*Today’s computers are so complex that they can only be designed and manufactured with slightly less complex computers. In turn the computers used for the design and manufacture are so complex that they themselves can only be designed and manufactured with slightly less complex computers. You’d have to go through many such loops to get back to a level that could possibly be re-built from scratch.*  
  
*Once you start to understand how our modern devices work and how they’re created, it’s impossible to not be dizzy about the depth of everything that’s involved, and to not be in awe about the fact that they work at all, when Murphy’s law says that they simply shouldn’t possibly work.*  
  
*For non-technologists, this is all a black box. That is a great success of technology: all those layers of complexity are entirely hidden and people can use them without even knowing that they exist at all.* 

[http://bretthard.in/post/dizzying-but-invisible-depth](http://bretthard.in/post/dizzying-but-invisible-depth)

comments.author: SmoggySPECTEREGaming
comments.body:
Honestly, I started my Vibecoding journey 6 months ago knowing less than the tip of the iceberg, but I've learned so much just by doing it. I started taking entry level fundamentals courses for python because I did find it fascinating. That said, I am still not, and will never truly be an expert. It's awesome. I know just enough to reiterate what I want in blender, meshy, tripo workflows, and then to be able to have Opus implement the systems I am going for with balancing is nothing short of remarkable.

The crazy part is, it will only continue to improve. This is the worst it will get.

Blender in particular was daunting for me to understand,  but through connecting MCPs, I am literally able to add something to the game, right it, and animate it within the span of 30 minutes. Just insanity.

With that in mind, my knowledge pales in comparison to others, and my game is nowhere near ready to see the light of day, but it will get there.

replies.author: jmontanholi
replies.body: Like, I am always acting as both director and QA, then balancing things and telling AI to fix bugs. I am going to start doing it as I do at work, do something, review files, commit. Work on another chunk, review, commit. Its slower, sure, but then its easier to understand your own project and be able to steer the AI in the right direction every time you review a file that it did something wrong

replies.author: First-Tutor-5454
replies.body: Why does that matter?

replies.author: jmontanholi
replies.body: It's a principle of code development, basically you make a class, that has all of the basic functionalities that you need for a given entity, a boss, an enemy, the player, projectiles, whatever. Then, if you want something that is like that but slightly different, you inherit from that class and make the changes on top. Now, why is this important? If you copy paste a full boss file 8 times and change them, you now have 8 full files to support, and if you discover a bug in one part that is common to all of them, you have to fix it in 8 places(or AI in this case) and now you have 8 possible places where you might forget to fix instead of 1

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
The whole point of vibecoding is that there is no balance. You just churn out stuff, and if it no longer fits, you rewrite it. You don't look at code.

Blind trust in iterating quickly and failing fast. That's the definition, at least. If you don't do that, you are not vibe-coding, but having AI assist your development to various degrees.

comments.author: KalElReturns89
comments.body:
I'm a software dev but I think balance went out the window. It's so inefficient to code anything yourself now.

You could look at what it's committing to make sure it's what you intended, but honestly the syntax is mostly solved.

The bigger things are learning where AI likes to cut corners and forcing it to follow best practices and do its own research. If you ask for recommendations on pros and cons of architecture decisions, that helps get you involved and more in the loop and making some human judgment calls.

comments.author: DrinkTeaFightMonster
comments.body:
Being the director and having enough bandwidth to say no is a huge job. The job is now being a good director.

Even on game teams, there are many good game directors who don't know a thing about engineering. That is not their job. To them, their job is to communicate to the engineers or engineering leads on what the game vision is. 

This is the same now -- you convey to the AI. 

You will be startled by how much good communication changes throughput. But also, it doesn't all just "happen". There are so many things you have to say NO to. Or guide them towards. Like working with real humans. 

I'd say as a whole, any AI game project needs you as a good director more than a good engineer.

comments.author: EdOfO
comments.body:
The more you know, the easier things will be to fix and modify later. Most programmers work more on architecture and algorithms solving the big stuff than they do writing 10,000 lines in one go. They fix tech debt (which you'll have a hell'va lot of) and refactor and bug hunt and such things. And all that is helpful if you want to excell. If you can do X, then they can do 5X or 10X.  
  
Anyway, it seems you answered your own question. "I want to be a person who understands what they've made."  
Great! You can do that! There are plugins and skills and all sorts of stuff you can do to make your development educational simultaneously as you go. Learn until you're satisfied. Idk where that point will be for you, but you will know.
